quiz_met1:1.q: A hepatocyte is building polysaccharides and lipids from sugars and fatty acids. Which term describes this process, and what happens to ATP and NADPH?
quiz_met1:1.r: Anabolism builds cell macromolecules from precursor molecules and spends the chemical energy carried by ATP, NADH, NADPH and FADH2; catabolism regenerates those carriers while breaking nutrients down to CO2, H2O and NH3 (p. 588).

quiz_met1:10.q: A sprinter runs 100 meters in about 9 seconds. Which reaction mainly regenerated her muscle ATP after the first 3 seconds?
quiz_met1:10.r: A 100 m sprint of 8 to 10 seconds runs on the phosphagen system: cellular ATP is used in 3 seconds and is regenerated for a few seconds more by the reaction between ADP and phosphocreatine (p. 602).

quiz_met1:11.q: Muscle glycogen supports ATP synthesis more than twice as fast as blood glucose. Which feature of glycogen helps explain this?
o: Lipolysis at the oil droplet surface
quiz_met1:11.r: Relative rates of ATP synthesis are phosphocreatine 100, glycogen by anaerobic glycolysis 55, glucose by aerobic glycolysis 23 and fatty acids 10; glycogen is fast because phosphorolysis forms G-1-P without using ATP and its tree structure gives many simultaneous reaction sites (p. 603).

quiz_met1:12.q: A cyclist is three hours into a continuous ride. Which fuel now supplies the largest share of his working muscle's oxygen uptake?
quiz_met1:12.r: Muscle glycogen dominates early (about 80% near 20 minutes) and then falls to about 10%, while fatty acids rise to about 60 to 65% between 2 and 4 hours and blood glucose sits near 25 to 30%; exercise lasting more than a few minutes uses a mixture of fuels (p. 604).

quiz_met1:13.q: A sedentary 49-year-old man finishes a 12-week exercise program and his peak VO2 rises by 68%. A muscle biopsy would most likely show increased markers for which organelle?
quiz_met1:13.r: As aerobic capacity (measured by VO2) improves, the number and size of mitochondria in skeletal muscle increase, giving more room for O2-dependent reactions (p. 606); this is the lecture's own opening case (p. 583).

quiz_met1:14.q: A patient's cells cannot generate enough NADPH from glucose. Which of the lecture's major pathways is impaired?
quiz_met1:14.r: The pentose phosphate pathway converts glucose to ribose and generates NADPH (p. 590).

quiz_met1:15.q: An infant lacks one enzyme in the middle of a metabolic pathway. Applying the lecture's blocked-pipe analogy, what is most likely to build up to potentially toxic levels?
o: Product just downstream of the block
Final end product of the pathway
quiz_met1:15.r: A blockage makes material back up behind it, like water behind a blocked pipe (p. 608); metabolic derangements lead to changes in flux and potentially toxic accumulation of intermediate (p. 610).

quiz_met1:2.q: A volunteer eats far more calories than his immediate needs. According to the lecture, in what form is this excess energy stored?
quiz_met1:2.r: Energy in excess of immediate needs is stored as glycogen or fatty acid, not as ATP; ATP is like an operating budget with just enough to cover expenses, and cells try to keep the ATP:ADP ratio constant (p. 597).

quiz_met1:3.q: Phosphohexose isomerase runs in the net forward direction during glycolysis and the net reverse direction during gluconeogenesis. What solely determines its direction?
o: The cellular ATP to ADP ratio
Relative levels of G6P and F6P
quiz_met1:3.r: The G6P to F6P isomerization has a standard free energy change near zero (1.7 kJ/mol), so it is readily reversible and its direction is based solely on the relative concentration of G-6-P and F-6-P (p. 593, p. 592).

quiz_met1:4.q: A drug that inhibits F-1,6-BPase halts hepatic gluconeogenesis even though every glycolytic enzyme is intact. Which property of the PFK1 reaction explains why it cannot simply run backward?
o: Free energy change close to zero
Operation at or close to equilibrium
quiz_met1:4.r: A reaction with a highly favorable free energy change is not likely to undergo direct reversal or reach equilibrium, so the pathway needs a separate bypass reaction to go in reverse (p. 594); PFK1 is the example, bypassed by F-1,6-BPase (p. 595).

quiz_met1:5.q: A membrane-free cell extract still makes ATP during glycolysis. Which molecule does the lecture give as the example of the phosphate donor in this type of ATP synthesis?
quiz_met1:5.r: In substrate-level phosphorylation the phosphate group is transferred to ADP from a high-energy phosphorylated substrate, and the slide's example is phosphoenolpyruvate (p. 598); free Pi is the phosphate source in oxidative phosphorylation instead (p. 599).

quiz_met1:6.q: A biochemist wants an ATP-generating process whose ATP yield per substrate is a measurable whole number. According to the lecture, which process fits?
quiz_met1:6.r: Substrate-level phosphorylation has measurable, whole-number stoichiometry between substrates and products (p. 598); oxidative phosphorylation lacks whole-number stoichiometry between reduced intermediate and ATP (p. 599).

quiz_met1:7.q: A poison completely blocks ATP synthase, yet the cell still phosphorylates some ADP by direct transfer from substrates. In which two pathways does this occur?
o: The TCA cycle and electron transport
quiz_met1:7.r: Substrate-level phosphorylation occurs during glycolysis and the TCA cycle (p. 598); ATP synthase belongs to oxidative phosphorylation (p. 599).

quiz_met1:8.q: In respiring mitochondria, electrons pass from NADH along carriers to oxygen with a favorable free energy change. What is that free energy directly used to do?
o: Split ATP into ADP and Pi
quiz_met1:8.r: The favorable free energy change of electron transfer is used to generate a H+ gradient, and release of that gradient then powers ATP synthesis from ADP and Pi (p. 599).

quiz_met1:9.q: Stored carbohydrate yields 4 kcal per gram dry but only 1 to 1.5 kcal per gram wet, while triacylglycerol yields 9 either way. According to the lecture's table, what accounts for this?
o: Fat needs no ATP for activation
Glycogen energy is lost as lactate
quiz_met1:9.r: Carbohydrate (and protein) carry 2 to 3 g of water per g dry weight, which drops them from 4 to 1 to 1.5 kcal/g wet weight, while triacylglycerol carries 0 g of water and stays at 9 kcal/g; triacylglycerol is also the largest store at 135,000 kcal against 840 kcal for carbohydrate (p. 601).

quiz_met1_b:1.q: ATP synthesis from ADP and Pi has a positive free energy change and will not proceed alone. According to the lecture, what allows cells to make ATP anyway?
o: Raising the ATP to ADP ratio
quiz_met1_b:1.r: Oxidation of glucose is strongly favorable (negative free energy change) and ATP synthesis from ADP and Pi is disfavorable (positive); the slide writes them as one coupled reaction, a favorable reaction driving a disfavorable one (p. 589).

quiz_met1_b:10.q: A swimmer's race lasts about 90 seconds, powered mainly by anaerobic breakdown of muscle glycogen. According to the lecture, what limits this energy system to several minutes?
quiz_met1_b:10.r: The glycogen-lactic acid system (swimmer, 400 m, 1.3 to 1.6 minutes) is anaerobic metabolism limited to several minutes by lactate accumulation (p. 602). Phosphocreatine belongs to the phosphagen system of the 8 to 10 second sprint.

quiz_met1_b:11.q: During a long hike, fatty acids supply ATP at the slowest relative rate of any fuel in the lecture. Besides transport and mitochondrial oxidation, what limits this rate?
o: Lipolysis only at the droplet surface
quiz_met1_b:11.r: Fatty acids have the lowest relative rate of ATP synthesis (10, against 100 for phosphocreatine, 55 for glycogen and 23 for glucose) because lipolysis occurs only at the interface between oil droplet and cytosol and is limited by transport and mitochondrial oxidation (p. 603).

quiz_met1_b:12.q: Muscle glycogen is cleaved by phosphorolysis, which forms glucose 1-phosphate without spending ATP. According to the lecture, how many ATP does anaerobic glycolysis then yield per glucosyl group?
quiz_met1_b:12.r: Because G-1-P is formed from glycogen without use of ATP, anaerobic glycolysis yields 3 ATP per glucosyl group (p. 603). The numbers 55 and 23 are relative rates for glycogen and glucose, and 38 is her ATP count for full oxidation of glucose (p. 589).

quiz_met1_b:13.q: Two cyclists ride for 60 minutes, one at heavy and one at moderate intensity. According to the lecture, about how much muscle glycogen remains in the moderate rider at that point?
quiz_met1_b:13.r: At 60 minutes heavy exercise has taken muscle glycogen to about 0%, moderate exercise to about 50% (it nears 0% at 120 minutes), and light exercise leaves it near 100%; muscle glycogen is used at different rates depending on intensity (p. 605).

quiz_met1_b:14.q: A hepatocyte accumulates glucose 6-phosphate behind a block in glycolysis. According to the lecture, besides glycogen synthesis, which pathway can take up this intermediate directly?
quiz_met1_b:14.r: On the pathway map glucose 6-phosphate is a branch point: it connects to glucose 1-phosphate and glycogen, to fructose 6-phosphate in glycolysis, and to gluconolactone 6-phosphate, the first step of the pentose phosphate pathway (p. 591). A block makes flux back up and spill into the other branches (p. 608).

quiz_met1_b:15.q: A child's enzyme defect lies in one pathway, yet the main finding is sluggish flux through a different pathway that seemed unrelated. Which of the lecture's analogies illustrates this situation?
o: Heavy rain overflowing the sewer dam
A budget with just enough for expenses
A blocked vent pipe slowing the drains
Savings kept in a bank account
Energy lost along the food chain
quiz_met1_b:15.r: A blockage of the vent pipe on the roof leads to slow drains and weak flushes elsewhere, so the source of the problem may not be where you expect (p. 609). The sewer overflow slide is about where material backs up behind a blockage (p. 608).

quiz_met1_b:2.q: A myocyte goes from rest to vigorous contraction, sharply raising its energy use. According to the lecture, which quantity does the cell try to hold constant?
quiz_met1_b:2.r: ATP is like an operating budget with just enough to cover expenses, and cells try to maintain a constant ATP:ADP ratio (p. 597, repeated on the review slide p. 610).

quiz_met1_b:3.q: An enzyme in hepatocytes normally operates close to equilibrium. If the concentration of its products suddenly rises, what happens to the reaction?
o: A bypass enzyme must take over
Flux is unchanged until ATP falls
quiz_met1_b:3.r: For a reaction at or close to equilibrium, more substrate shifts it toward products and more product shifts it toward substrates, so it is readily reversible (p. 592). Only highly favorable reactions need a separate bypass (p. 594).

quiz_met1_b:4.q: A mutant hepatocyte keeps PFK1 and F-1,6-BPase fully active at the same time. According to the lecture, what results?
o: A futile cycle that spends ATP
quiz_met1_b:4.r: Opposing reactions must be coordinately controlled, otherwise a futile cycle results; the slide title shows the net effect, F6P plus ATP going to F6P plus ADP and Pi (p. 595). Cells avoid this with separate compartments or allosteric regulators.

quiz_met1_b:5.q: A membrane-free extract makes ATP only by direct phosphate transfer from substrates. Adding intact mitochondria lets it also make ATP using electrons from which pair of reduced intermediates?
quiz_met1_b:5.r: In oxidative phosphorylation the reduced intermediates NADH and FADH2 pass electrons to carriers of increasing reduction potential (p. 599). Substrate-level phosphorylation needs no electron donor, only a phosphorylated substrate (p. 598).

quiz_met1_b:6.q: A drug makes the inner mitochondrial membrane freely permeable to H+ while electron transfer to oxygen continues. Why does ATP synthase stop making ATP?
o: No H+ gradient is left to release
NADH can no longer donate electrons
Oxygen is no longer reduced to water
The ATP to ADP ratio stays constant
quiz_met1_b:6.r: Electron transfer builds a H+ gradient, and it is release of that gradient that powers ATP synthesis from ADP and Pi (p. 599). With a leaky membrane the electrons still flow but no gradient is left for ATP synthase.

quiz_met1_b:7.q: A poison blocks the step of oxidative phosphorylation in which oxygen is reduced to water. According to the lecture, which component carries out this step?
quiz_met1_b:7.r: On the slide the cytochrome oxidase complex is the last carrier, where H+ and O2 form H2O (p. 599). The order drawn is NADH dehydrogenase, ubiquinone, cytochrome b-c complex, cytochrome c, cytochrome oxidase complex, then ATP synthase.

quiz_met1_b:8.q: A student compares substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis with oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria. According to the lecture, which feature do both share?
o: A H+ gradient drives the reaction
quiz_met1_b:8.r: Both make ATP by adding phosphate to ADP: from a high-energy phosphorylated substrate in substrate-level phosphorylation (p. 598) and from Pi, powered by the H+ gradient, in oxidative phosphorylation (p. 599). The gradient, NADH and the lack of whole-number stoichiometry belong to oxidative phosphorylation only.

quiz_met1_b:9.q: A 70 kg man has just eaten. According to the lecture, which order ranks his energy stores from most to least total kcal?
quiz_met1_b:9.r: Total energy stored is 135,000 kcal as triacylglycerol, 24,000 kcal as protein and only 840 kcal as carbohydrate in a 70 kg man who has recently eaten (p. 601).

Met 1: Energetics and Generation of ATP (Jones) high-yield tables

Met 1: Principles of Energetics and Generation of ATP (Jones). You scored 24/30 on this lecture in September. Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF, where the lecture runs pp. 579 to 610. Everything is from her slides unless labeled (outside the slides). The slides never spell out ATP, ADP, Pi, NAD, NADH, NADP, NADPH, FAD, FADH2, CoA, TCA, PFK1, PFK2, F2,6-BP, PKA, VO2 or the pathway-map abbreviations, so those expansions are standard names (outside the slides).

1. Anabolism, catabolism and the carriers that link them (LO 1)

Catabolism breaks nutrients down and charges adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and the reduced cofactors, and anabolism spends them to build macromolecules (p. 588).

2. Reversible versus irreversible reactions (LO 2)

A reaction near equilibrium follows substrate and product concentrations, and a reaction with a very negative free energy change needs a separate bypass to go backward (p. 592, p. 594).

Table 2a. Reversible versus "irreversible" (p. 592, p. 594, p. 610)

Feature Reversible "Irreversible"
Free energy change as written ΔG ± 0 ΔG << 0
In words At or close to equilibrium Highly favorable free energy change

Direct reversal Readily reversible Not likely under normal physiologic conditions
More substrate (A, B) Shifts toward products Not stated
More product (P, Q) Shifts toward substrates Not stated
To run the pathway in reverse Same reaction runs backward Needs a separate bypass reaction
Regulation Not stated Often regulatory targets
Slide wording "Readily REVERSIBLE" "May be functionally IRREVERSIBLE"

3. Substrate-level versus oxidative phosphorylation (LO 3)

Substrate-level phosphorylation hands a phosphate from a substrate straight to ADP, and oxidative phosphorylation uses electron transfer to build a H+ gradient that drives ATP synthesis (p. 598, p. 599).
